query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-annealing treatment in air at high temperature induces the formation of a thin, Mn/Si-enriched native oxide scale on Q235 low‐carbon steel that serves as an effective diffusion barrier against aggressive molten salt environments at high temperatures, while offering little to no benefit (or possibly even reduced protection) at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 low‐carbon steel in its as-received, pre-exposure state
generation.intervention: Pre-annealing in air at approximately 700 °C for varied durations (e.g., 1–10 hours) to produce a reproducible, continuous native oxide scale enriched with minor alloying oxides (such as Mn and Si oxides) on the surface
generation.conditions: Hot corrosion tests in molten salt environments (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) at 700–900 °C in parallel with room-temperature corrosion assessments under controlled laboratory conditions
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, composition, and adhesion quality of the pre-formed native oxide scale (a mixture of iron oxides with minor Mn and Si oxide phases) that develops during the annealing process
generation.mechanism: High-temperature annealing promotes selective oxidation of Q235 steel’s surface whereby minor alloying elements (Mn and Si) segregate to form a mixed oxide scale that is more continuous and adherent. This scale acts as a diffusion barrier to corrosive species under hot corrosion conditions, limiting further oxidation and degradation. In contrast, at room temperature, the oxide scale formed may be less protective due to differences in phase stability and adhesion, leading to differences in corrosion performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under hot corrosion conditions at 700–900 °C, pre-annealed Q235 steel is expected to exhibit a lower mass change and less surface degradation (e.g., reduced spallation or pitting) compared to untreated Q235 steel. Under room-temperature exposure, the improvement (or protective effect) may be weak or absent because the oxide scale structure and stability that are beneficial at high temperatures are not as effective under ambient conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel that develops a native oxide scale only under ambient conditions without controlled pre-annealing
generation.boundary: The protective effect is anticipated only when the pre-annealing treatment produces a continuous, adherent oxide layer; if the treatment is too short (insufficient scale formation) or too long (leading to scale thickening and potential spallation), the mechanism may not apply. Additionally, the mechanism is expected to be significant under high-temperature, aggressive molten salt conditions and may not translate to lower-temperature corrosion regimes.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal annealing time and exact oxide composition required to maximize protection, as well as the long-term mechanical stability (e.g., resistance to spallation) of the pre-formed oxide scale during thermal cycling. Moreover, the comparative performance at room temperature may vary depending on ambient corrosion kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set undergoing the controlled air annealing at 700 °C for durations varying between 1 and 10 hours, and a reference set with no such treatment. Expose both sets to a molten salt corrosion environment (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) at 700–900 °C for a fixed duration, as well as to room-temperature corrosion tests under identical exposure times. Characterize the surface oxide scale (using XRD, SEM/EDS) and measure mass change and degradation features (e.g., spallation, pitting) before and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via XRD, EDS)
Extent of scale spallation or pitting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-annealed Q235 steel samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in mass change and degradation (or show comparable or worse corrosion behavior) under hot molten salt conditions relative to untreated samples—and if the formed oxide scale does not demonstrate enhanced continuity or adhesion—then the hypothesis that the pre-formed Mn/Si-enriched oxide scale is responsible for superior high-temperature corrosion protection is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As is known, metallic niobium has a low oxidation temperature in an oxygen-containing environment (less than 600 °C) with the formation of an oxide film on the surface, the thickness of which increases with increasing annealing time or temperature. As can be seen from the data presented, in the case of Nb alloy samples after thermal testing, the surface is a mixture of an oxide film, the thickness of which is at least 500–700 nm in the case of the original sample and somewhat less (no more than 500 nm) in the case of the irradiated sample. At the same time, the structure of this oxide film for the original sample and the irradiated one has obvious differences. In the case of the initial sample, the oxidized layer is represented by a mixture of grain inclusions that make up the porous film, while for the irradiated samples, the oxide film delamination is observed with the formation of extended voids. When vanadium, tantalum, and titanium were added to the niobium alloy, the formation of oxide inclusions was not observed as a result of high-temperature tests. AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. proposals.material_system: Q235 low-carbon steel in its pre-exposure state
proposals.intervention: Controlled pre-annealing in air to induce a reproducible, thin native oxide scale enriched in minor alloying elements (e.g., Mn/Si oxides)
proposals.conditions: Anneal at 700 °C for varying times (e.g., 1–10 h) in air before subjecting to hot-corrosion tests in molten salt environments (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl at 700–900 °C) and parallel room-temperature corrosion tests
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation and adherence quality of the native oxide scale comprising mixed iron oxides and minor spinel phases
proposals.mechanism: The controlled high-temperature anneal triggers selective oxidation that forms a continuous, adherent, protective oxide scale. This scale retards further corrosive attack by acting as a diffusion barrier; its composition (influenced by the presence of Mn and Si) differs from that formed at room temperature, explaining the regime-dependent performance.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed to produce a robust, adherent oxide scale will show reduced mass change and lower corrosion degradation under hot corrosion conditions relative to untreated Q235, whereas room-temperature exposure may show less protection if the oxide is less effective.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the effect of a pre-formed oxide scale on corrosion protection, testing whether its formation (and stability) under hot conditions governs retention of protection or promotes degradation, directly linking processing-induced structural changes to performance.

proposals.material_system: Q235 low-carbon steel with inherent ferrite-pearlite microstructure
proposals.intervention: Heat treatment to homogenize the microstructure (via austenitizing and controlled cooling) to eliminate microstructural heterogeneities
proposals.conditions: Heat Q235 steel to 900 °C to form austenite followed by controlled furnace cooling to achieve a uniform ferrite/pearlite distribution; compare with as-received Q235 under identical hot-corrosion tests (molten salt exposure at 800–900 °C) and room temperature corrosion assessments
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduction in localized galvanic couples and differential oxidation sites due to homogenization of the ferrite and pearlite phases
proposals.mechanism: In the untreated state, the inherent heterogeneous microstructure promotes localized galvanic corrosion and uneven oxide scale formation. By homogenizing the microstructure, the distribution of phases becomes more uniform, potentially resulting in a more continuous and conformal oxide scale that offers improved corrosion protection in high-temperature regimes.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Homogenized Q235 samples will exhibit a more uniform and protective oxide layer, lower weight loss, and fewer spallation events during hot corrosion tests compared to non-homogenized samples, while differences at room temperature will be minimal if the oxide kinetics differ.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study will isolate the role of microstructural heterogeneity in governing the corrosion protection failure or retention, providing a testable mechanistic hypothesis on how microstructure influences the oxide scale’s performance in differing temperature regimes.

proposals.material_system: Q235 low-carbon steel with residual stresses from manufacturing
proposals.intervention: Application of a stress-relief heat treatment to modify or eliminate residual stresses prior to corrosion exposure
proposals.conditions: Perform a low-temperature stress-relief anneal (e.g., 550–600 °C for 1–2 h) on Q235 steel specimens before exposure to high-temperature hot-corrosion conditions (molten salt exposures at 700–900 °C) and compare against as-received samples
proposals.structural_mediator: Modification of residual stress levels in the bulk and at the oxide/metal interface
proposals.mechanism: Residual stresses can induce micro-cracking in the nascent oxide scale during thermal cycling, undermining the integrity of the protective barrier. Stress relief should reduce crack initiation/propagation, leading to a more stable oxide layer that better resists hot corrosion, while at room temperature the effect might be less pronounced due to lower thermo-mechanical strains.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Stress-relieved samples are expected to show improved oxide scale adherence, lower incidence of crack-induced spallation, and overall reduced corrosion degradation under hot corrosion conditions, compared to untreated Q235 steel.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By isolating the effect of residual stresses on oxide integrity and corrosion behavior, this study targets a mechanistic hypothesis that links processing-induced mechanical factors to corrosion protection or failure in differing temperature regimes, providing clear criteria for falsification if no significant differences are observed.

proposals.material_system: Q235 low-carbon steel with typical inclusion populations (e.g., MnS inclusions)
proposals.intervention: Comparison of Q235 steels produced via conventional vs. ultra-low inclusion processing, possibly supplemented by post-process inclusion modification (e.g., via controlled annealing to alter inclusion morphology)
proposals.conditions: Prepare two sets of Q235 samples: one with standard inclusion content and one with significantly reduced inclusion density; subject both to identical hot-corrosion (700–900 °C molten salt) and room-temperature corrosion tests
proposals.structural_mediator: Presence, distribution, and morphology of non-metallic inclusions that act as localized corrosion initiation sites
proposals.mechanism: Non-metallic inclusions such as manganese sulfides can serve as preferential sites for oxide nucleation and induce localized stress concentrations that undermine the protective oxide scale. Reducing inclusion content or modifying their characteristics should result in a more homogeneous oxide coverage and enhanced corrosion resistance, particularly under high-temperature cyclic conditions.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Ultra-clean Q235 with reduced or modified inclusion populations will display a more continuous oxide scale and superior corrosion resistance (i.e., lower mass loss and fewer spallation areas) during hot corrosion tests compared to conventionally produced Q235 steel, with potential minimal differences at room temperature if corrosion kinetics are less aggressive.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study isolates the role of micro-scale heterogeneities (inclusions) in governing the initiation and propagation of corrosion processes, providing a clearly testable hypothesis on how such features impact the protective behavior across temperature regimes; an absence of expected differences would directly falsify the proposed mechanism.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes – it isolates a specific microstructural feature (non-metallic inclusions) that may govern oxide nucleation and local stress, thereby affecting corrosion protection across both room and high‐temperature regimes.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system (Q235 steel) and the test conditions (hot corrosion at 700–900 °C and room-temperature tests).
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; inclusions like MnS are well-known to act as localized corrosion initiators or stress concentrators that can disrupt oxide scale formation.
critiques.feasibility: Processing Q235 to reduce inclusions (or modify them via annealing) in parallel with conventional samples is feasible with established metallurgical techniques.
critiques.evidence: Some studies (e.g., record PMC10864269) highlight microstructural modifications via processing, and related work shows that refining particles can improve corrosion resistance, though direct inclusion-specific experiments on Q235 are minimal.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that inclusions may not be the dominant factor controlling corrosion behavior – other microstructural aspects might mask their effect, limiting the clarity of the mechanistic link.
critiques.fix: Include additional microstructural characterization (e.g., quantitative inclusion mapping before and after annealing) to ensure that differences in inclusion populations are the primary variable affecting corrosion performance.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes – it targets the influence of inherent microstructural heterogeneity (ferrite/pearlite distribution) on the formation and conformity of the oxide scale under differing temperatures.
critiques.constraints: The approach strictly uses Q235 steel and modifies its microstructure via heat treatment, fitting within the specified conditions for hot-corrosion and room-temperature corrosion testing.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis is physically plausible because local galvanic couples between ferrite and pearlite can affect oxidation kinetics and oxide scale uniformity.
critiques.feasibility: Austenitizing and controlled cooling to achieve a homogenized microstructure are well-established heat treatment practices.
critiques.evidence: Literature (e.g., PMC9498077 and related corrosion studies) supports the idea that microstructural homogenization can alter corrosion behavior, though the direct application to Q235 under these regimes is novel.
critiques.main_risk: The risk lies in potential competing phenomena such as precipitation during homogenization that might affect oxidation behavior, thereby complicating the isolation of microstructural heterogeneity as the key factor.
critiques.fix: Refine the heat treatment protocol to minimize unintended precipitate formation and include phase analysis to confirm that only homogenization (and not other microstructural alterations) is influencing the corrosion behavior.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes – it provides a testable hypothesis on whether a controlled, pre-formed native oxide scale influences the protective behavior under hot- and room-temperature corrosion regimes.
critiques.constraints: The approach complies with the material system (Q235 steel) and uses experimental conditions aligned with both high-temperature molten salt tests and room-temperature corrosion assessments.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of a pre-formed oxide scale acting as a diffusion barrier is physically sound, with the note that the oxide scale composition (e.g., Mn/Si oxides) can significantly affect barrier properties.
critiques.feasibility: Pre-annealing in air to establish a native oxide is a common technique and can be reliably controlled over time and temperature.
critiques.evidence: Support comes from studies (e.g., PMC10488378) that demonstrate controlled oxidation leading to improved high-temperature oxide stability, although similar direct experiments on Q235 are not extensive.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the oxide scale formed by pre-annealing might not resist spallation or further degradation under the aggressive molten salt conditions, thereby obscuring the link between the pre-exposure state and later corrosion performance.
critiques.fix: Introduce adhesion and mechanical integrity measurements of the pre-formed oxide scale to ensure its stability during subsequent molten salt exposure and to clearly correlate oxide quality with corrosion resistance.

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially – the hypothesis examines whether residual stresses affect oxide scale integrity and thereby influence corrosion. However, it is less directly linked to the primary material degradation mechanisms (i.e., microstructure or pre-formed oxide layer) emphasized in the question.
critiques.constraints: While it uses Q235 steel and tests similar corrosion conditions, the focus on residual stresses does not decisively address the mechanistic cause of corrosion-protection failure inherent to the pre-exposure state.
critiques.physical_soundness: The idea that residual stresses can lead to oxide scale cracking is physically plausible; however, in Q235 steel the variation in residual stress may be a secondary rather than dominant factor.
critiques.feasibility: Stress relief heat treatments are widely used and the experimental design is feasible with standard metallurgical practices.
critiques.evidence: Some evidence (e.g., PMC8200011 and PMC9955357) indicates that stress-related phenomena can influence coating cracking and degradation, though these studies typically focus on coatings and high-entropy alloys rather than pristine Q235.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that residual stress relief may not significantly alter the corrosion behavior if the degradation is more strongly controlled by chemical or microstructural factors, reducing the experiment's ability to isolate the governing mechanism.
critiques.fix: Combine stress measurements (e.g., X-ray diffraction residual stress analysis) with detailed observations of oxide morphology to more directly correlate stress relief with changes in corrosion behavior, thereby strengthening the mechanistic link.
